summary: PCE is a key component of software-defined networking. This informational document describes an architecture in which PCE and PCEP are used in a network with central control, so a central controller can compute and update paths as the network or demand changes.

plainLanguage.summary: A Path Computation Element (PCE) can calculate paths using information about the network and its resources. This RFC describes how a PCE-based controller can use PCEP to direct network elements, with or without a distributed control plane.

subtitle: Using a PCE-based controller and PCEP to direct network elements from a central point.

tldr.problem: Software-Defined Networking needs a way to compute paths and program network devices, including networks that still use a distributed control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a hybrid architecture in which a PCE-based controller uses PCEP to communicate with network elements, either directly or alongside their control plane.
tldr.outcome: It describes an architecture and possible areas of applicability but defines no protocol extensions or detailed use cases.

today: RFC 8283 is an Informational document published in December 2017. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: From Path Computation to Central Control
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) was developed to compute paths for MPLS traffic-engineered networks. Its role later expanded to other uses, including delegated control and PCE-initiated use of network resources.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) uses a central controller to program network devices. This RFC considers the PCE as the component that plans how traffic uses network resources and PCEP as a protocol for the controller to communicate with network elements.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE computes paths through a network. This RFC describes how it can also be part of a central controller that programs network devices.

sections.title: A Hybrid Controller Architecture
sections.content:
An orchestrator or management system asks the PCE-based controller to create connectivity. The controller uses topology and resource information in its Traffic Engineering Database to compute paths, then sends requests to network elements using PCEP.

The RFC describes a hybrid design: the controller can speak PCEP to individual network elements and can also work with devices that use a control plane to establish connections. This avoids requiring a separate network controller with a different southbound protocol, while allowing deployments to retain a control plane where it is useful.
sections.plainLanguage: A management system asks the controller for connectivity. The controller computes paths and uses PCEP to tell network elements what to establish.

sections.title: Scaling and Resilience
sections.content:
The RFC describes three approaches to controller scaling and resilience. A partitioned network assigns each controller a subset of the network, which reduces its workload but requires coordination for end-to-end connections. Parallel controllers can each control all network elements, but they need to synchronize state.

A hierarchical design uses a parent controller to coordinate child controllers. It can help with scaling and connections across domains, but the RFC notes that hierarchy alone does little to protect against controller failure. Deployments may combine these approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can divide work among controllers, use parallel controllers, or arrange controllers in levels. Each approach has trade-offs in workload, coordination, and protection from failure.

sections.title: Possible Uses
sections.content:
The RFC lists possible uses across control-plane-operated MPLS and GMPLS, static LSPs, multicast, transport SDN, segment routing, and Service Function Chaining. It also lists functions such as traffic engineering, traffic classification, and service delivery.

This list is introductory. The RFC does not claim that central control is required or recommended for every use, and it leaves detailed use cases and any protocol extensions to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE-based controller may support several kinds of networks and traffic-management tasks. The RFC lists possibilities but does not recommend central control for every network.

sections.title: Protocol, Security, and Manageability
sections.content:
PCEP already includes a request for a PCE to initiate an LSP and a report from a network element. The RFC expects that use cases may need additional information in PCEP messages, while aiming to keep extensions backward compatible and identifiable as profiles.

A central controller can become a point of failure and a target for denial-of-service, interception, or message modification. The RFC points to PCEP security features and TLS-based mechanisms, and notes that the controller needs reliable information about network nodes, links, and state. This document requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A central controller needs protected PCEP connections and accurate network information. If the controller fails or is attacked, it can affect management of the network.
